# Packaging & release

How the desktop app is built into installers, how updates are published, and how
to do either by hand.

Server-side deployment (Docker, multi-process, env vars) is a different topic —
see [operations.md](./operations.md).

Installers are produced by electron-builder, driven by
[apps/desktop/scripts/electron-builder.mjs](../../apps/desktop/scripts/electron-builder.mjs).
The build configuration is generated by
[apps/desktop/scripts/lib/build-config.mjs](../../apps/desktop/scripts/lib/build-config.mjs)
rather than checked in, because three things about a release are only known at
build time: the update channel, whether signing credentials exist, and which
architecture the server's native modules were compiled for. JSON cannot express
any of them.

---

## 1. What you get

| Platform | Targets | Update manifest |
| -------- | ------- | --------------- |
| Windows | `nsis` installer, `portable` exe | `<channel>.yml` |
| macOS | `dmg`, `zip` | `<channel>-mac.yml` |
| Linux | `AppImage`, `deb`, `rpm` | `<channel>-linux.yml` |

Everything lands in `apps/desktop/release/`.

Each installer carries the full stack: the Electron shell, the web SPA, the
server bundled to a single file, and that server's native dependencies compiled
against Electron's ABI. There is no separate runtime for a user to install.

---

## 2. Two constraints

**Build on the platform you are targeting.** electron-builder refuses outright
to build macOS anywhere but macOS (`Build for macOS is supported only on
macOS`), and the Linux `deb`/`rpm` targets shell out to local packaging tools.
There is no cross-compilation path, and neither WSL nor a container changes the
macOS answer.

**The installer architecture must match the staged server runtime.** The
embedded server ships real `.node` binaries compiled for one CPU. Asking for an
installer of a different architecture is refused rather than silently producing
an app whose database fails on first use.

---

## 3. Prerequisites

Beyond Node 22 and pnpm 10:

| Platform | Needs |
| -------- | ----- |
| Windows | nothing extra |
| macOS | Xcode Command Line Tools (`xcode-select --install`) |
| Linux | a C++ toolchain and the deb/rpm tooling (below) |

```bash
# Linux only
sudo apt-get install -y python3 make g++ rpm fakeroot dpkg-dev
```

`python3 make g++` are not optional on Linux: node-pty publishes no Linux
prebuild, so it compiles from source during staging. electron-builder downloads
`fpm` itself, but `rpm`, `fakeroot` and `dpkg-dev` must be present.

---

## 4. Build installers

```bash
pnpm install
pnpm package:desktop
```

That is the whole thing for your current OS and CPU.

It runs three stages, which you can also run individually when only one needs
rebuilding:

```bash
pnpm --filter @generatorai/web build             # 1. web SPA
pnpm --filter @generatorai/desktop build         # 2. Electron main + preload + icons
pnpm --filter @generatorai/desktop build:server  # 3. bundle the server, then install
                                                 #    its native deps for Electron's ABI
```

then invokes electron-builder.

To inspect the payload without paying for installer compression:

```bash
pnpm --filter @generatorai/desktop package:dir   # → release/<platform>-unpacked/
```

### Stage 3 in more detail

`build:server` is where most of the packaging risk lives. It bundles the server
to one file with esbuild, then generates a manifest and runs `pnpm install
--prod` against it in a staging directory — rather than copying `node_modules`
out of the monorepo, which would mean reimplementing module resolution and
shipping pnpm's symlinks. See
[apps/desktop/scripts/stage-server-runtime.mjs](../../apps/desktop/scripts/stage-server-runtime.mjs).

It then asserts the result: every runtime package present, no symlinks, and a
loadable native binary for each native dependency. A mis-staged tree otherwise
installs cleanly and fails on the user's machine.

---

## 5. Building for a different architecture

The native modules must be staged for the target CPU first, so this is two steps
rather than a flag:

```bash
pnpm --filter @generatorai/web build
pnpm --filter @generatorai/desktop build

GENERATORAI_STAGE_ARCH=arm64 pnpm --filter @generatorai/desktop build:server
pnpm --filter @generatorai/desktop electron-builder --arm64
```

PowerShell:

```powershell
$env:GENERATORAI_STAGE_ARCH='arm64'
pnpm --filter @generatorai/desktop build:server
pnpm --filter @generatorai/desktop electron-builder --arm64
$env:GENERATORAI_STAGE_ARCH=$null
```

Skipping the re-stage is a hard error, not a broken installer:

```
[electron-builder] --arm64 was requested but the server runtime is staged for x64.
        Set GENERATORAI_STAGE_ARCH=arm64 and re-run `pnpm run build:server`.
```

macOS is built per-architecture for the same reason, rather than `universal`: a
universal app has to carry both slices of every native module, and the server
runtime is staged for one at a time.

---

## 6. Update channel

A local build takes its channel from the version in
[apps/desktop/package.json](../../apps/desktop/package.json). In CI the tag
decides, and is passed down as `GENERATORAI_RELEASE_CHANNEL` so a build and the
release it lands in can never disagree.

| Version / tag | Channel | GitHub release |
| ------------- | ------- | -------------- |
| `0.0.1-alpha.3` | `alpha` | pre-release |
| `0.1.0-beta.1` | `beta` | pre-release |
| `1.0.0` | `latest` | full release |

`alpha` and `beta` are not free-form. electron-updater's GitHub provider
hardcodes those two names when deciding whether a pre-release is a valid
upgrade, so a custom channel (`nightly`, say) would strand testers with no route
back to stable.

The channel also names the manifest, which is what stops someone on the stable
channel being offered an alpha build: electron-updater only reads the manifest
matching its own channel.

---

## 7. Where updates come from

The publish target is derived from `GITHUB_REPOSITORY`, which GitHub Actions
sets to the repository actually running the workflow — so it cannot drift the
way a checked-in `owner/repo` does through a rename, transfer or fork.

A local build without it produces no update feed at all, which is correct:
there is nothing for it to poll.

| Variable | Purpose |
| -------- | ------- |
| `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` | `owner/repo` to publish updates from |
| `GENERATORAI_UPDATE_REPOSITORY` | Overrides the above when releases live elsewhere |
| `GENERATORAI_UPDATE_URL` | Points the build at a generic feed instead (see §10) |
| `GENERATORAI_RELEASE_CHANNEL` | Overrides the channel derived from the version |
| `GENERATORAI_STAGE_ARCH` / `GENERATORAI_STAGE_PLATFORM` | Target for the staged server runtime |
| `GENERATORAI_MAINTAINER` | `Name <email>` for the deb/rpm headers |
| `GENERATORAI_HOMEPAGE` | Homepage for the deb/rpm headers |

```bash
GITHUB_REPOSITORY=owner/repo pnpm package:desktop
```

> [!NOTE]
> The `VAR=value command` prefix is bash/zsh. In PowerShell set the variable
> first (`$env:GITHUB_REPOSITORY='owner/repo'`), then run the command.

`GENERATORAI_MAINTAINER` and `GENERATORAI_HOMEPAGE` only matter on Linux: `fpm`
refuses to build a `deb` or `rpm` without a homepage and an RFC-822 maintainer.
Both default to values derived from the publish target, using GitHub's no-reply
address form.

---

## 8. Signing

Credentials are all-or-nothing per group. Supply every variable in a group to
sign, or none to build unsigned. A half-configured group fails the build rather
than quietly producing an unsigned artifact that looks fine — which is the
failure mode you would otherwise discover after publishing.

| Platform | Required together |
| -------- | ----------------- |
| Windows | `CSC_LINK`, `CSC_KEY_PASSWORD` |
| macOS | `CSC_LINK`, `CSC_KEY_PASSWORD`, `APPLE_API_KEY`, `APPLE_API_KEY_ID`, `APPLE_API_ISSUER` |
| Linux | not signed |

macOS treats its certificate and notarization credentials as one unit: a signed
but un-notarized build is still refused by Gatekeeper on first launch, so having
one without the other is never useful.

Empty variables count as absent. `CSC_LINK: ${{ secrets.CSC_LINK }}` expands to
an empty string when the secret does not exist, and electron-builder would
otherwise treat that as "signing requested".

> [!IMPORTANT]
> An unsigned macOS build cannot auto-update — Squirrel.Mac rejects a signature
> it cannot verify. The build therefore withholds `<channel>-mac.yml` rather
> than advertising an update path that fails on every client. Unsigned macOS
> builds are manual-download only, regardless of what the release pipeline does.

---

## 9. Verify before shipping

```bash
pnpm verify:release
```

electron-updater trusts the manifest completely, so a target that overwrites
another's output invalidates it without failing the build. This re-hashes every
artifact and compares it against the manifest. CI runs it on each platform.

To exercise the packaged app itself — it launches the real executable, boots the
embedded server, and checks the native database module actually loads:

```bash
pnpm --filter @generatorai/desktop package:dir
node agent-tests/packaged-app-smoke.mjs
```

---

## 10. Testing auto-update locally

The update path otherwise only runs on a user's machine, days after the build
that produced it. Serve a release directory and point a build at it:

```bash
# terminal 1 — serves apps/desktop/release by default
pnpm --filter @generatorai/desktop mock-update-server

# terminal 2 — bake the local feed into the app
GENERATORAI_UPDATE_URL=http://localhost:8770 pnpm package:desktop
```

The packaged app will poll `http://localhost:8770` on launch. Bump the version
and rebuild to see an update offered, and check `app-update.yml` inside
`release/<platform>-unpacked/resources/` to confirm the feed was baked in.

---

## 11. Publishing a release

Releases are tag-driven; see [release.yml](../workflows/release.yml).

```bash
git tag v0.0.1-alpha.2
git push origin v0.0.1-alpha.2
```

The workflow then:

1. **prepare** — resolves channel, tag and prerelease flag once, and rejects a
   malformed tag before three platform builds are spent on it.
2. **preflight** — build, lint, typecheck, test and the security invariants. A
   tag cannot publish an untested build.
3. **build** (3-OS matrix) — packages with `--publish never`, then verifies the
   manifest, then uploads artifacts.
4. **release** — downloads every platform's artifacts and creates one GitHub
   release.

Builds never publish directly. Three matrix legs racing to create the same
release is a documented way to end up with duplicates or a half-populated
release, so artifacts are collected and published once.

`workflow_dispatch` is also available if you need to pick the channel manually.
